title: Is a working at heights ticket mandatory in Australia?
seoTitle: Working at heights duties in Australia
description: No licence exists for working at heights in Australia. What model WHS Regulations 78 to 80 require: fall controls, rescue procedures and suitable training.
shortAnswer: No. There is no licence or mandatory ticket for working at heights under Australia's model Work Health and Safety Regulations. Instead, regulations 78 to 80 require a business to manage fall risks, work on the ground or a solid construction where reasonably practicable, then use fall prevention, work positioning or fall arrest in that order, and set up, test and train workers in rescue procedures whenever fall arrest is used.
keyTakeaways: Regulation 78 applies to any fall from one level to another that is reasonably likely to cause injury. There is no minimum height in regulation 78 itself.

Regulation 79 sets a fixed order of controls: fall prevention device, then work positioning system, then fall arrest system, each only if the one before is not reasonably practicable. Training is listed as an example of a safe system of work.

Regulation 80 is the only falls provision that names training: where fall arrest is used, the business must establish emergency and rescue procedures, test them, and train every worker who uses the system or may initiate a rescue.
The 2 metre figure comes from regulation 291: construction work with a risk of falling more than 2 metres is high risk construction work and needs a safe work method statement.

A high risk work licence is needed only for specific plant and tasks, such as scaffolding over 4 metres or boom type elevating work platforms of 11 metres or more, not for working at height generally.
jurisdiction: Australia (model WHS laws, adopted in all jurisdictions except Victoria)
regulator: State and territory WHS regulators applying the model Work Health and Safety Regulations and the model Code of Practice: Managing the risk of falls at workplaces developed by Safe Work Australia
appliesTo: Persons conducting a business or undertaking (PCBUs) where workers could fall from one level to another
Construction, maintenance, warehousing, transport, agriculture and utilities businesses
Workers using fall arrest harnesses, restraint systems or work positioning systems such as rope access
Supervisors and workers who may initiate or carry out a rescue

sections.heading: Is there a working at heights licence in Australia?

blocks.text: No. The model WHS Regulations contain no licence, card or mandatory course for working at heights. Part 4.4, Falls, imposes duties on the business to control the risk, and Part 4.5 licenses specific high risk work, but working at height as such is not a licensed activity. Course certificates commonly called a working at heights ticket are evidence of training, not a legal permit.

That does not make training optional. The general requirement in regulation 39 that information, training and instruction be "suitable and adequate" for the work, the risks and the controls applies in full, as described in [the WHS Act duty to provide training](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training). What the law does not do is prescribe the course.

blocks.title: Currency and jurisdiction
blocks.text: This page reflects the model WHS Regulations published by Safe Work Australia on December 5, 2025 and the model Code of Practice: Managing the risk of falls at workplaces (October 2018 edition), as at November 2026. Each jurisdiction adopts the regulations and approves the code under its own law, and penalty amounts for tier E offences differ. Victoria has its own regime; see the [Victorian construction induction and licensing page](/regulations/victoria-construction-induction-and-hrw-regime).

Regulation 78 of the [model WHS Regulations](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-12/model-whs-regulations-5_december_2025.pdf) requires a PCBU to manage, under the risk management process in Part 3.1, risks associated with "a fall by a person from one level to another that is reasonably likely to cause injury". It names five situations: an elevated workplace, the vicinity of an opening, the vicinity of an edge, a surface a person could fall through, and any other place from which a person could fall.

Regulation 78(3) requires that, so far as is reasonably practicable, work with a fall risk is carried out on the ground or on a solid construction. A solid construction is defined as an area with a surface able to support all persons and things on it, barriers around the perimeter and openings, an even and readily negotiable surface and gradient, and a safe means of entry and exit. Regulation 78(4) separately requires safe access to and exit from the workplace and each fall risk area.

sections.heading: What order of fall controls does regulation 79 set?

blocks.text: If the fall risk cannot be eliminated, regulation 79 requires the PCBU to minimize it by providing and maintaining a safe system of work in a set order.

items: A fall prevention device, if reasonably practicable. The regulation lists a secure fence, edge protection, working platforms and covers.
If not, a work positioning system, such as a travel restraint or industrial rope access system.
If neither is reasonably practicable, a fall arrest system, so far as is reasonably practicable.

blocks.text: The examples attached to regulation 79(3) include "providing training in relation to the risks involved in working at the workplace", safe work procedures, safe sequencing, safe use of ladders, permit systems and signs. A combination of controls may be used if one is not enough. Regulation 79 does not apply to stunt work, acrobatics, theatrical performances, sporting or athletic activities, or horse riding, which are managed under regulation 36 instead.

sections.heading: What training does regulation 80 require when fall arrest is used?

blocks.text: Regulation 80 is the specific training obligation in Part 4.4. Where a PCBU uses a fall arrest system as a control, it must establish emergency procedures, including rescue procedures, for the use of the system; ensure the procedures are tested so that they are effective; and provide relevant workers with suitable and adequate information, training and instruction in those procedures. Each duty carries a tier E maximum penalty.

Relevant workers are defined broadly: anyone who uses or is to use a fall arrest system, and anyone who may be involved in initiating or implementing the emergency procedures. A ground crew member who never wears a harness but would call or carry out the rescue is therefore in scope.

The [model Code of Practice](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-10/Model%20Code%20of%20Practice%20-%20Managing%20the%20Risk%20of%20Falls%20at%20Workplaces%2021102022_0.pdf) adds that rescue training should start the rescue immediately, avoid putting rescuers at risk, and set its frequency by "the worker's competence and their ability to retain competence through regular exposure" to the equipment and skills. It sets no fixed interval, so the business must justify the one it chooses.

sections.heading: What should working at heights training cover?

blocks.text: The model Code of Practice states that workers must be trained and have the skills to carry out a task safely, and that training should be provided by a competent person. For workers exposed to falls from any height, it lists the content that training should include.

items: Proper use, wearing, storage and maintenance of personal protective equipment.
The hazards and risks of the work, and how to follow the procedures, including any safe work method statement.
Why each fall protection measure is in place and how to use it properly.
Emergency and rescue procedures, and how to report fall hazards and incidents.
Correct selection, fitting, use, inspection, maintenance and storage of fall arrest and restraint equipment where it is used.
Other hazards present, such as electrical hazards or crushing from elevating work platforms.

blocks.text: The code also says supervisors should be trained, that only workers trained in the system of work should be authorized to do it, and that users and supervisors of work positioning systems "should undertake a relevant competency based course of training" before use, because those systems need a high level of competency.

sections.heading: Where do the 2 metre rule and licences fit in?

blocks.text: The 2 metre figure is a construction trigger, not a falls threshold. Regulation 291 defines high risk construction work to include construction work that "involves a risk of a person falling more than 2 metres". That work needs a safe work method statement and SWMS based instruction, covered in [construction SWMS training](/regulations/construction-swms-and-high-risk-construction-work-training). Below 2 metres, and outside construction, regulations 78 to 80 still apply.

Licences apply to particular plant. The model code notes that scaffolding from which a person or object could fall more than 4 metres must be erected, altered and dismantled by a scaffolding licence holder or a supervised trainee, while Schedule 3 of the model Regulations makes operating a boom type elevating work platform with a boom of 11 metres or more a licensed class; see [high risk work licence requirements](/regulations/high-risk-work-licence-requirements). Construction workers must also hold a [general construction induction card](/regulations/general-construction-induction-white-card).

blocks.text: The most common audit gap is regulation 80: a harness course certificate exists, but there is no site rescue plan, no record that it was tested, and no training record for the people expected to perform the rescue. A [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) on the site's actual anchors and rescue kit addresses all three.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry breaks falls training into the knowledge points the Code lists, then links each to the control actually used on site, so a worker on edge protection and a worker on rope access receive and are assessed on different content. Rescue roles are modeled separately from harness users. See how this applies to [energy and resources organizations](/industries/energy-resources).

faqs.q: Does a working at heights certificate expire?
faqs.a: The model WHS laws set no expiry because they do not require the certificate. Providers often print a recommended refresher date. The legal test is whether training remains suitable and adequate, and for rescue, the Code links frequency to the worker's ability to retain competence through regular exposure.

faqs.q: Is a harness always required above 2 metres?
faqs.a: No. Regulation 79 puts fall arrest last. A business must first consider working on the ground or a solid construction, then fall prevention devices such as guardrails, edge protection or working platforms, then work positioning, and only then fall arrest.

faqs.q: Do the falls regulations apply in Victoria?
faqs.a: No. Victoria has not adopted the model WHS laws. Fall prevention in Victoria is governed by the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 and the Occupational Health and Safety Regulations 2017, with their own provisions and compliance codes.
